notes.meaning: Paul faces a question people often asked about his teaching. If God gives more grace—His free, undeserved favor—whenever sin increases, should Christians keep on sinning on purpose? He asks this to show how wrong it is to treat God's forgiving love as a license to do evil.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern teachers promote a view often called hyper-grace, claiming that since God's grace covers every sin, believers do not need to focus on turning away from sinful habits.

notes.meaning: Paul answers the question with a strong and shocked denial. Believers have died to sin, which means its power over them has been broken. A person who has died to something cannot go on living inside it as if nothing changed.

Paul appeals to what Christians experienced when they were baptized. Baptism marks a person's public connection to Jesus Christ and His people. Being baptized into Jesus means sharing in His death on the cross, cutting our tie to the old way of life.

differ.view: Baptists generally understand this as a spiritual baptism that joins the believer to Christ by faith, while water baptism is an outward picture that does not itself save or wash away sin.
Presbyterian and Reformed churches teach that baptism is a covenant sign and seal through which the Holy Spirit truly gives the promised grace of union with Christ to believers.
Lutherans teach that baptism is a real means of grace in which God Himself connects the person to the saving benefits of Christ's death and gives new birth.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic Church teaches that the sacrament of baptism removes original sin and infuses new life into the soul, uniting the person directly to Christ's saving death.

notes.meaning: Going into the water of baptism represents being buried with Christ, showing that the old sinful life has ended for good. Just as God the Father used His glorious power to raise Jesus from the grave, believers are raised up to live a brand-new kind of life. Our daily actions should show the new life God has placed inside us.

differ.view: Lutherans teach that baptism is not just a picture or a symbol, but a "means of grace"—a physical tool God uses to give His free favor and forgiveness. In this view, God uses the water and His Word together to bury our sinful nature and give us new spiritual life in Christ.

Reformed Christians teach that water does not automatically save someone, because salvation comes through faith alone. Instead, baptism is a "sacrament"—a sacred sign and seal, like an official royal stamp—that visibly confirms God’s promise to unite His people to Jesus’ death and resurrection.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Baptism is a sacrament that actually washes away original sin, joining the soul to Christ and infusing the new life of grace.

notes.meaning: Paul uses the picture of a branch grafted into a tree to show how closely believers are joined to Jesus. Because Christians are united with Him in a death like His, they will certainly share in His resurrection life too. This shared life gives believers the power to follow God today and the promise of bodily life in the future.

Our old self means who we were before knowing Christ, shaped by the sinful nature passed down from Adam. That old self was put to death on the cross with Jesus so that sin would lose its grip over our physical bodies. Because of this, Christians are no longer trapped as helpless slaves to sin.

differ.view: Methodists view the crucifixion of the old self as a progressive work in the believer, where the inward power of sin is gradually put to death over time.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic theology teaches that baptism wipes away original sin, but an inner inclination toward sin remains that calls believers to ongoing spiritual battle.

notes.meaning: When an enslaved person dies, their former master no longer has any claim or authority over them. In the same way, because believers died with Christ, they have been released from sin's legal claim and tyrannical rule. We are declared free in God's sight from sin's right to command us.

Paul states that if we died with Christ, we can be confident that we will also share His life. This life begins right now as we walk in obedience and will be made complete when our bodies are raised at His return. Believers can live with peace, knowing their spiritual future rests on Jesus.

Jesus was raised from the dead and will never die again. When He willingly gave Himself up to the grave, He broke its power forever, so death has no mastery over Him now. Because our life is tied to the risen Christ, the life He gives us cannot be lost to the grave.

When Jesus died, He died to deal with sin once for all, paying the full penalty and breaking its power forever. He never needs to suffer on the cross again. The life He now lives is an unbroken, glorious life directed completely toward God the Father.

Paul tells Christians to reckon—which means to count or consider as true—that they are dead to sin but alive to God. This does not mean pretending something is true, but trusting what Jesus actually accomplished for us. We are called to live every day knowing that sin does not own us and that our lives belong to God.

Since sin has lost its right to rule, Christians must not let it sit on the throne of their mortal bodies. Our earthly bodies still experience selfish cravings, but we do not have to obey them. Believers are told to put up a fight and refuse to let evil desires direct their lives.

Believers must not hand over their hands, eyes, tongues, or thoughts to be used as tools for doing wrong. Instead, they should offer their whole selves to God as people who have been brought from death into life. Every part of our body can then become a weapon used for what is good and pleasing to Him.

Sin will not be our ruler, because Christians are not under the law but under grace. The law pointed out what was right and showed human guilt, but it could not provide the strength to obey. Grace pardons our sins and gives us the Holy Spirit so we have the power to live pleasing lives.

Paul asks if being under grace gives Christians an excuse to commit sin now and then. He rejects this thought immediately with the strongest words. Grace does not free us to disobey God; it sets us free from the trap of sin so we can follow Him.

Paul points out a basic rule of life: whoever you obey becomes your true master. If someone chooses to obey sin, they are enslaved to sin, and that path leads straight to spiritual death. If someone chooses to obey God, that obedience leads to righteousness, which is right living that honors Him.

Paul thanks God because the Roman Christians have turned away from their old slavery to sin. They did not just agree with Christian teaching in their heads, but they welcomed it from the heart. The true gospel acted like a mold, reshaping their thinking and desires to match God's will.

When God set believers free from sin's tyranny, He did not leave them without any direction. Instead, they became willing servants of righteousness. Serving God's goodness is the only place where human beings find real freedom and peace.

Paul explains that he uses the everyday picture of slavery because human minds struggle to grasp deep spiritual truths. In the past, people offered their bodies to dirty habits and growing wickedness. Now they should offer their bodies just as eagerly to righteousness, which leads to holiness, a life set apart for God.

When people lived as slaves to sin, they did not feel bound to do what was right, and they produced no goodness for God. They thought they were free, but they were completely controlled by their evil desires. Paul reminds them of this past to show how completely one master shuts out the other.

Paul asks believers what good fruit or real profit their old sinful life ever brought them. Those sinful choices produced nothing good and now leave them feeling deep shame. The final outcome of living for sin is eternal death, which means being separated from God forever.

Now that believers are set free from sin and serve God, their lives produce the good fruit of holiness. Growing in this holy character leads in the end to eternal life with God. Serving the Lord brings a clean conscience now and unending joy in the world to come.

Sin pays its servants wages, and those earned wages are death and eternal loss. On the other hand, eternal life is not something a person can work for or earn; it is the free gift of God found in Jesus Christ our Lord. We earn our own ruin, but God freely gives us salvation in His Son.
